newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka hails new Indian prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka hails new Indian prime minister.

text.p: Sri Lanka on Monday welcomed the swearing in of India's new Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, calling him an old friend who will further strengthen ties between the two neighbours.
"... there could be no more fitting choice to lead India in this, its 50th anniversary year of independence," President Chandrika Kumaratunga said in a message to Gujral.
"We in Sri Lanka have enthusiastically welcomed the significant impetus you imparted to the further strengthening of the long-standing close and friendly ties between our two countries," she said.
Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar said he believed that under Gujral's leadership ties between the two countries "will enter a period of unparalleled strength and mutual benefit."
A foreign ministry spokesman earlier described Gujral as a sincere friend of Sri Lanka who understood the country well.
"He has even in the worst of times, as was in 1989, been able to steer Indo-Sri Lanka relations out of trouble," he said.
"We have no doubt that the solid foundation he has helped lay as foreign minister will be further consolidated now that he is the prime minister of India," he added.

Indo-Sri Lanka relations touched a low in the late 1980s after Indian troops arrived in the island to try to disarm rebels of the Liberation Tigers of Tiger Eelam (LTTE) under a controversial agreement between the two countries.
The troops were withdrawn in mid-1990 after suffering heavy casualties and failing to defeat the rebels. Gujral was then foreign minister of India.
Sri Lankan newspapers said on Monday that Gujral would be able to reduce regional tension by forging closer ties with Pakistan and China.
The Observer said in a front-page editorial that Gujral was a firm believer in defusing tensions with neighbours and was keen on "nurturing trust and confidence".
Gujral visited Colombo in January, during his second stint as foreign minister, and said India was ready to do anything to help bring the island's 13-year-old ethnic conflict to an end.
He also promised to lift trade barriers to help increase Sri Lankan exports to its huge neighbour as part of what is now known in diplomatic circles as the "Gujral Doctrine".
This holds that as the largest nation in South Asia, India can afford to offer concessions to its neighbours in the interests of regional harmony.
